opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we think about a lot, because it's partly a scientific question and partly a practical, resource question.

Ideally, you'd want to train a Scientist AI from scratch, because the whole point is that the system's training objective is different from what we do today. Current frontier models are pretrained to imitate human text, which already brings in human-like goals and agency, and then they're further trained with reinforcement learning to please us or achieve goals, and that's where many of the worrying behaviors come from: deception, sycophancy, self-preservation-like tendencies. The Scientist AI idea is to have a system whose job is to model the world and produce calibrated probabilities, explanations of the data, not to act or to please. If you start from a model that has already absorbed agentic tendencies, it's not obvious that fine-tuning can fully remove them. It might just paper over them, the way safety fine-tuning today can often be bypassed.

On the other hand, training from scratch at frontier scale costs an enormous amount of compute and money, and a nonprofit research effort can't compete with the big labs on that right away. And we need to show that the approach works and is competitive in capability, otherwise nobody will adopt it.

So I think the sensible path is staged. First, smaller-scale experiments where we can train from scratch and really test the core ideas: does this kind of training objective give us honest, well-calibrated predictions, and do we avoid the emergence of hidden goals? In parallel, fine-tune existing open-weight models as a cheaper way to demonstrate useful properties, for example as a guardrail that estimates the probability that a proposed action causes harm, and rejects it if that probability is too high. That's useful even if the underlying model isn't perfectly clean, because the monitor's role is narrower.

Then, if the results are convincing, the argument becomes much easier to make to governments, philanthropists, or companies that it's worth investing in a from-scratch, frontier-scale version. Fine-tuning is a way to get evidence and usefulness quickly; training from scratch is where I think the stronger safety guarantees ultimately have to come from.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning may not remove existing agentic tendencies and that stronger safety guarantees should come from training from scratch, but does not state that fine-tuning forfeits a mathematical guarantee.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's really a practical question more than a philosophical one, at least for now. The honest answer is that we don't have the resources to train frontier-scale models from scratch, and I'm not sure we should want to, at this stage. The point of what we're doing with Scientist AI is to demonstrate that you can build a system that is genuinely non-agentic, that is trained to understand the world and to produce honest, calibrated explanations and predictions, rather than to pursue goals or to please the user. And you can make a lot of progress on that question by starting from existing pre-trained models.

So my view is that fine-tuning is the right place to start, because what matters most in the near term is the training objective and the way the system is used, not necessarily every bit of the pre-training. If you take a strong base model and then you train it, not with the usual reinforcement learning from human feedback which rewards imitation and sycophancy, but with objectives that push towards estimating probabilities of statements, towards being uncertain when it should be uncertain, towards explaining rather than acting, then you can already test the main scientific claims. Does the model become more honest? Does it stop trying to convince you of things? Can it serve as a guardrail that evaluates whether an action proposed by some other agentic system is likely to cause harm? Those are questions we can investigate without spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

That said, I think there are limitations to fine-tuning, and we need to be clear-eyed about them. A base model trained on human text has absorbed a lot of human-like patterns, including the tendency to behave like an agent, to have something like persona, to want to be agreeable. Fine-tuning can suppress some of that, but we know from the research on jailbreaks and on what happens under distribution shift that these behaviours can come back. So if you really want strong guarantees, if you want a system where you can argue that it does not have hidden goals, then I think eventually you need to think about training from the ground up with objectives that never reward agency in the first place. That is the longer-term agenda, and it would require a lot more compute and probably collaboration with large labs or governments.

So I see it as a staged approach. First, fine-tune, to validate the ideas and show that the direction is scientifically sound and useful, for example as a safety layer. Then, as we learn and as resources allow, move towards training that incorporates these principles from scratch. And I would add that the demonstration itself matters for a different reason: I want to show other researchers and policymakers that there is an alternative to the current race to build ever more agentic systems. If a small nonprofit can show a credible path with modest means, that changes the conversation about what is possible.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different objectives here. If you want to demonstrate the basic ideas and learn quickly, then fine-tuning an existing model is a very attractive starting point. Training a large model from scratch is expensive, and a lot of what you need—the ability to understand language, for example—is already there. So you can use that foundation to experiment with a system whose role is to propose hypotheses, evaluate evidence, and express uncertainty, rather than to take actions to achieve some goal.

But there’s a limitation: fine-tuning doesn’t give you a clean slate. You’ve inherited whatever was learned during the original training, and changing the model’s observable behaviour doesn’t establish that you’ve removed all the tendencies you’re concerned about. So a successful demonstration would be useful evidence, but it wouldn’t, by itself, establish safety.

Training from scratch gives you more control over the objective and the training process. That matters if we want a stronger connection between the mathematical principles behind Scientist AI and the system we actually build. But it’s not a guarantee either; we still have to understand how well our training procedure approximates those principles.

So I would see these as complementary. Start with existing models to test the ideas and find the problems, while developing the methods that would justify a more carefully controlled training effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should explore both, because they answer somewhat different questions. If you start from an existing model, you can make progress much faster and at much lower cost. You can test whether it can represent competing hypotheses, express uncertainty, and make predictions without being trained to take actions in the world. That’s a useful way to develop the methodology.

But fine-tuning has a limitation: the model has already acquired tendencies from its previous training. If part of that training encouraged it to act like an agent, you can’t simply assume that fine-tuning has removed those tendencies. You might get the behaviour you want in your tests without having established the underlying safety properties.

Training from scratch gives you more control over the objective and the training process. It lets you investigate whether those properties arise by construction. But it’s much more expensive, especially if you want to demonstrate something at the frontier of capabilities.

So I would use existing models to learn quickly and build demonstrations, while also doing experiments from scratch, initially at smaller scales. The important thing is to distinguish demonstrating useful behaviour from establishing that the system is safe.
